# cache

Policies for deciding which key to drop when a cache is full. A cache holds
at most `capacity` keys, so when a new one arrives something has to go, and
which one is the whole question. The difference between a good and a bad
eviction rule on the same workload is routinely ten points of hit rate, for
identical memory and near-identical cost per operation.

Each is implemented against the same tiny interface and measured on the same
four traces.

## Choosing one

| If you need | Use | Because |
|---|---|---|
| One good default | **[SIEVE](sieve/)** | Scan-resistant, no lock on a hit, and the simplest thing here that is genuinely good. |
| The highest hit rate | **[W-TinyLFU](w-tinylfu/)** | A frequency sketch turns admission into a contest the incumbent usually deserves to win. |
| Web or CDN traffic full of one-hit wonders | **[S3-FIFO](s3-fifo/)** | Most objects die in a small probation queue without ever touching the main cache. |
| To survive workload shifts without retuning | **[ARC](arc/)** | Adapts its own recency/frequency split as the workload moves, but check the patent history. |
| Scan resistance you can explain in a sentence | **[2Q](2q/)** | A key must come back after eviction to earn the main cache. |
| LRU without a write on every hit | **[CLOCK](clock/)** | One reference bit and a sweeping hand approximate the same order. |
| The default nobody will question | **[LRU](lru/)** | The baseline everything else here is measured against, and a scan flushes it. |
| Stable popularity, with scans passing through | **[LFU](lfu/)** | Ranks by lifetime frequency. The price is that it cannot forget. |
| Predictable eviction, or hits that cost nothing | **[FIFO](fifo/)** | Ignores reuse entirely. It is the floor everything else must beat. |

If you have no information about your workload, start with [SIEVE](sieve/). If
you have measurements and want the last few points,
[W-TinyLFU](w-tinylfu/). If your workload's popular set moves,
[ARC](arc/).

## Traces

Four canonical workloads, generated from a seed rather than downloaded, so every
language reproduces them event for event. The full specification is in
[`TRACES.md`](../../packages/core/src/domains/cache/TRACES.md).

| Trace | What it is | What it separates |
|---|---|---|
| `zipf-1.0-100k` | 100,000 accesses over 10,000 keys, Zipf α=1.0 | The everyday case, where most good policies land close together |
| `zipf-0.75-1m` | 1,000,000 accesses over 100,000 keys, Zipf α=0.75 | Flatter and longer: a larger working set spreads policies out |
| `scan-heavy` | Zipf 1.0 with a sequential sweep every 20,000 accesses | Scan-resistant policies from LRU and CLOCK |
| `shifting-popularity` | Zipf 1.0 whose popular set rotates every 25,000 accesses | Policies that can forget from those that cannot |

### Reading the table

**The gap to OPT is the prize.** No online policy can beat the offline bound, so
the distance between the best row and the OPT row is everything still available
on that workload. On `zipf-1.0-100k` that gap is about seven points. On
`zipf-0.75-1m` it is fourteen, which is why the flatter trace is the more
interesting benchmark.

**`shifting-popularity` is where the field separates.** Every policy scores
respectably on the stationary Zipf traces because they all converge on caching
roughly the same popular set. Watch [LFU](lfu/) collapse when the popular set
rotates: it holds yesterday's winners and cannot be persuaded otherwise. That
one column is worth more than the other three for choosing a policy.

**LFU and SIEVE tie to the last digit on the stationary traces, and it is not
rounding.** On `zipf-1.0-100k` and `scan-heavy` the two make bit-identical
decisions at every event: same hits, same victims, all the way down. Under
stationary skew, eviction pressure is always absorbed by entries that have
never been hit, and both policies then reduce to "evict the oldest never-hit
key". They are genuinely different policies: a uniform-random trace splits
them within about fifty evictions, and `shifting-popularity` is a two-times
gap in the table above. The tie is a property of the traces, worth knowing
before reading two identical rows as a copy-paste mistake.

**SIEVE is the one policy that falls below the FIFO floor.** It does so on
`shifting-popularity`, and only there. Its visited bit grants a second chance to
keys from the *previous* popular set, so at capacities large relative to how
fast popularity moves it holds stale entries that plain FIFO clears on schedule.
At smaller capacities the effect reverses. This is the kind of result a
benchmark table exists to surface: SIEVE is an excellent default and this is a
real edge where it is not, and neither fact is visible from the algorithm's
description.

**Identical numbers are not necessarily a bug.** [LFU](lfu/) and
[SIEVE](sieve/) record exactly the same hit rate on three of the four traces.
They are genuinely different policies: at smaller capacities they diverge and
end with different resident sets. But on a stationary Zipf workload with
capacity at 10% of the keyspace, both converge on caching the same top keys, and
therefore serve the same number of hits. The fourth column shows how different
they really are.

**Throughput is not in this table.** It is recorded in each policy's
`bench.json` and shown on its own page, but it is machine-dependent and is never
asserted. Choose on hit rate and on the operational
properties in the table above: whether a hit takes a lock, and what a scan does
to you.

## The interface

Every policy here implements the same contract, small enough to reimplement in
an afternoon:

```ts
interface CachePolicy<K> {
  onAccess(key: K, hit: boolean, meta?: CacheMeta): void
  evict(): K
  admit?(key: K, meta?: CacheMeta): boolean
}
```

No wall-clock access, no hidden randomness, no I/O. See
[`interface.ts`](../../packages/core/src/domains/cache/interface.ts).
